sections.html: Nerites (Neritidae), also known as racing snails, are very popular for their beautiful coloration and their excellent properties as algae cleaners. If enough specimens are kept, they reliably keep the aquarium glass clean. Plants are left completely alone.

There is no unwanted mass reproduction, as the larvae of these snails can only develop in the sea. The only downside of nerites are the white, chalky egg capsules that they attach to solid objects everywhere.
Vittina have separate sexes, so there are males and females, although they cannot be distinguished externally.

Many unanswered questions can probably only be resolved when more aquarists become involved in breeding these snails. This requires a saltwater aquarium. The adult snails live exclusively in fresh and brackish water. It would be proof of species identity if eggs from a breeding group with phenotypic zebra snails spontaneously grew into tractor snails.

Nerite snails became known in Europe very early on, as their pretty shells have always been used as jewelry. Vittina turrita was originally described in 1791 under the name Nerita turrita, later transferred to the genus Neritina, where it was listed in the subgenus Vittina until recently. In a major review of the nerites, Vittina was elevated to genus rank (Eichhorst, 2016).

Aquarists are usually guided by the shape and color of the shell, the coloration of the underside and the operculum. These characteristics are completely identical in the zebra snails and the onion or tractor snails. The latter, which derives one of its popular names from its shell pattern reminiscent of tractor tire imprints, is currently considered a valid species, Vittina semiconica, after having been considered a synonym of V. turrita for many years. Both forms come from the same supplier in Indonesia.
Eichhorst, T. E. (2016): Neritidae of the World, Vol. 2. ConchBooks, 672 pp.
